lesson.title: Fair or unfair models
lesson.subtitle: Check the errors for every group

video.title: Fair or unfair models: Check the errors for every group
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: We tried an app that listens to pupils read aloud and scores them. Overall it was right nine times in ten. But pupils from the village were marked down far more often.
Today: how a model can be good on average and still unfair to some pupils.
A model is biased when its mistakes fall more on one group than another. The average can look fine while one group carries most of the errors. So we check every group separately.
Split the test pupils by group and work out the error rate for each one. If one group's rate is much higher, the model is not fair to them, whatever the overall score says.
Here are the app's errors for each group of pupils. Town pupils had six wrong scores per hundred, while village pupils had twenty two.
Most bias starts in the data. The app learned from recordings of town voices, so village accents were rare in its training. A model can only be as fair as the examples it learned from.
We did three things. We stopped using the app's score for any decision, we sent the company recordings from our village pupils, and a teacher now listens whenever the app gives a low score.
Quick check! The app is right ninety percent of the time overall. Does that show it is fair to every group of pupils?
No. A good average can hide one group with many more errors. You only see bias when you check every group separately.
In the app, open the bias lab. Change how many examples of each group are in the training data, and watch each group's error rate.
Your turn. Where does most bias in a model start?
In the data it learned from. Remember: averages hide unfairness, so compare errors group by group, fix the data, and keep a person in the loop.
Try it in class tomorrow: give groups a made-up table of a model's results for boys and girls, or two classes. Ask them to work out the error rate for each group and decide whether the model is fair.
